content.tagline: A dirty panel loses up to two thirds of its output. A robot brings it back
content.descriptor: Chinese maker of robots and brushes for solar panel cleaning; own plant, national high-tech enterprise status
about: BeiJing Multifit Electrical Technology Co., Ltd. manufactures cleaning equipment for solar panels. Headquarters in Beijing, plant in Shantou (Guangdong), branches in Shenzhen and Sichuan. The company holds national high-tech enterprise status and trades under the MULTIFIT name.

The problem this equipment solves is measured in money. Dust, bird droppings and rust particles cut a panel's output to 20–36% of nominal; after cleaning, efficiency returns to 90–95% and falls again if maintenance stops. Beyond lost output, soiling is physically dangerous: a shaded section overheats, hot spots form, the panel degrades and can burn out. Cleaning is therefore not cosmetic — it extends the life of the plant.

The range splits in two. Robots: the MR-G series for single and double panel rows, the MR-T1 and MR-XY series, and the MR-AR transport trolley that moves a robot between rows. MULR brushes — from hand models to a water-driven version — cover the places where a robot is overkill. For every model the company provides a performance calculation: cleaning area per hour, daily rate, and the time needed for an array of a given size.

lines.name: MR-G — robots for panel rows
lines.note: The core series, in single-row and double-row versions. Travel speed around 12 m/min; throughput and daily rate are calculated for the specific array.

lines.name: MR-T1 / MR-XY
lines.note: Robot series for other plant configurations, differing in working width and operating mode; chosen by the geometry of the array.

lines.name: MR-AR — transport trolley
lines.note: Carries a robot between panel rows and removes the manual repositioning step. Needed where rows are many and set apart.

lines.name: MULR — cleaning brushes
lines.note: A brush range from hand models to a water-driven version. The answer for spots where a robot is excessive or cannot reach.

catalog_notes: First-generation robot travelling along the panel row: aluminium body, gaps up to 20 mm, slopes up to 8°.
Second generation: eight running wheels, removable anti-corrosion body, LFP battery rated for 4,000 cycles; 20 mm gaps, slopes up to 8°, panels 990–2384 mm.
Third generation: stainless-steel body, gaps up to 50 mm, slopes up to 20°, swinging head and all-wheel drive; remote range up to 400 m.
Double-roller-brush variant: finishes the edge of the PV row and suits arrays assembled from several panel rows.
Tracked robot for rows without bridge connections: 1-metre brush, dry and wet cleaning, joints up to 60 mm, slopes up to 25°, remote up to 400 m.
The fully automatic version of MR-T1: AI algorithms and visual recognition, path planning and posture correction.
Up-and-down robot for multi-row arrays up to 10 m wide; 8–12 m/min speed, remote control.
Rail-type transfer vehicle: moves the robot between rows in two to three minutes — roughly ten times faster than manual handling.
Manual scraper brush on a 3.5–7.5 m telescopic rod: two water outlets, adjustable head angle; panels, glass facades, snow.
Single-head electric brush for smaller arrays: soft bristles, head angle adjusts to the panel slope.
Double-head electric brush: two motors, water spray, 280 mm discs; grid or battery power, 4–6 hours of work.
Second generation of the double-head brush: 170 W brushless motors, 25.6 V 25 Ah battery, carbon-fibre rods of 3.5–7.5 m.
Rolling electric brush: 650 mm roller of 130 mm diameter, 400 rpm, three water outlets, water-blocking brush.
Second-generation rolling brush: 200 W, 420 rpm, forward/reverse rotation, polycarbonate housing.
Water-driven brush: powered by line pressure up to 7 MPa with no electricity; 125 or 350 mm discs, optional 2.2 kW pump.
